meta.title: Netflix traffic to SK Broadband, and the fight over who pays
meta.note: Only two traffic measurements were reported publicly. The line between them is interpolation, not data.

steps.title: Netflix arrives
steps.body: Foreign streaming lands on a network that was already finished. Korea had spent a decade building capacity; Netflix was the first company to really use it.

steps.title: 50 Gbps
steps.body: SK Broadband later put Netflix traffic on its network at 50 gigabits per second in May 2018. At the time, unremarkable.

steps.title: Netflix sues first
steps.body: Netflix asks a Seoul court to confirm it has no obligation to pay network usage fees, rejecting SK Broadband's demand. The argument is net neutrality: subscribers already pay for their broadband.

steps.title: The court disagrees
steps.body: Seoul Central District Court rules for SK Broadband, finding it reasonable that Netflix provide something in return for the service. Netflix appeals a month later, warning the ruling could topple the global internet ecosystem.

steps.title: 1,200 Gbps
steps.body: Twenty-four times the 2018 figure, driven by a run of hits. Squid Game had launched that same month. SK Broadband files a counterclaim seeking roughly 23 million dollars a year.

steps.title: Seven percent of everything
steps.body: By the first round of litigation Netflix accounted for at least 7% of all South Korean internet traffic, on figures from the Korea Information Society Development Institute. The disputed sum for a single year was 27.2 billion won.

steps.title: Both sides walk away
steps.body: After five years, Netflix and SK Broadband drop every claim and announce a partnership bundling Netflix with SK Telecom plans instead. No public agreement on the question itself. SK Broadband's position on network usage fees, it said, remains unchanged.
